In the modern digital age, the shift toward algorithmic governance suggests a world where human bias is replaced by the cold, mathematical precision of code. From credit scoring to judicial sentencing, automated systems are being integrated into the very fabric of institutional decision-making. The promise is one of efficiency and radical neutrality, (A)____ away the subjective whims of human administrators. However, this perceived neutrality is often illusory; algorithms are, after all, trained on historical data that inevitably (B)____ the prejudices of the past. If the training data contains systemic biases against certain demographics, the machine learns those patterns as “truths”. Far from eliminating discrimination, the algorithm may simply hide it behind a veneer of technical objectivity. Should a predictive policing system be designed to identify high-risk neighbourhoods, it might inadvertently codify and amplify existing systemic inequalities. By targeting areas that were already over-policed due to historical bias, the system creates a feedback loop. The “math” then appears to justify the (C)____ targeting of those same communities, creating a cycle that is difficult to break. (D)____ these tools offer undeniable efficiency in processing vast amounts of data, they lack the “moral imagination” required for true justice. A machine can identify a statistical correlation, but it cannot understand the nuance of human circumstance or the socio-economic context behind a data point. It treats humans as static variables rather than evolving individuals. This creates a dangerous (E)____ where the pursuit of objective fairness results in the automated replication of historical harm. As we outsource our judgement to software, we risk losing the ability to hold systems accountable. We must ensure that the drive for technological progress does not come at the expense of the very equity we seek to achieve.

question:
Fill in the blank.

Phenomenology suggests that time is not a series of discrete, ticking moments but a continuous, indivisible flow of consciousness. We do not experience life as a succession of “nows” like beads on a string. (A)____, our consciousness “protends” and “retains”, pulling the past and the future into every single instant of awareness.

Our perception of a “now” is constantly (B)____ by our memories of what has just occurred and our anticipations of what is about to happen. When you listen to a melody, you don’t hear isolated notes; you hear the relationship between the note playing now and the ones that preceded it. The “now” is always pregnant with the “next”.

Were we to experience a moment in total isolation, stripped of all context and memory, it (C)____ to have any human meaning. It would be a “flash” without a narrative, a sensation without a self. Our very identity is built upon the temporal continuity that phenomenology seeks to describe and analyse.

While objective clocks measure seconds with mechanical precision, the “lived time” of the individual is notoriously elastic. An hour spent in a state of flow can feel like minutes, while a minute of intense physical pain can feel like an eternity. The clock is a social (D)____; the experience of duration is a biological and psychological reality.

This subjective stretching of duration is what makes a moment of joy feel fleeting and a moment of dread feel interminable. We are not mere observers of time; we are the medium (E)____ which time gains its quality. To understand the human condition, we must look beyond the stopwatch and into the shifting currents of internal experience.

Choose the correct adverb to begin the sentence: (A)
